checkpoints: Envelope includes an event type field, letting a consumer route/dispatch without parsing the payload.
Envelope includes the payload itself — the actual event data being carried.
Envelope includes a client-supplied id, used for duplicate detection/idempotency downstream.
Envelope includes a timestamp, for ordering, debugging, and replay windows.

Partition key should be the entity that needs ordering (e.g., userId) and travels in the envelope as the routing key, since Kafka hashes the key to the same partition, keeping that entity's events strictly ordered relative to each other.
Trade-off: an unusually hot entity (whale key) causes its partition to absorb a disproportionate share of traffic while others sit idle, so key cardinality matters as much as which entity it names.

Topic granularity trade-off: one broad shared topic is simple to operate and trivially replayable by any new group but couples every domain's events into the same physical log and its retention/partition-count decisions, while per-domain topics isolate each team's schema and scaling at the cost of multiplying topics/consumer groups to manage — the right choice follows who actually consumes and who needs to replay, not a default.

The design relies on Kafka being append-only with each consumer group tracking its own offset, letting a future team add a new group and replay the entire history from the start with no code change or resend from the producer.
Routing: a genuine processing failure is published to the DLQ and then the offset is committed, isolating the poison message and freeing the partition immediately.
A duplicate is committed/skipped and never dead-lettered; conflating the two either loses a real message or head-of-line-blocks the whole partition through infinite retry.
The DLQ envelope must carry the original payload plus key, so an on-call engineer knows exactly which event this is.
The envelope must also carry the failure reason (exception message/type), the source topic/partition/offset, the attempt count, and a timestamp — missing any of these turns replay into guesswork.
Safety on replay relies precisely on the pipeline's existing idempotency mechanism (same clientMessageId, same Redis SETNX + Postgres unique constraint), not a promise to "only replay once."
On replay the consumer treats the message like any normal request: it processes it if the message never succeeded, and it dedups and skips automatically if it already succeeded.
Operability requires alerts on DLQ depth and on the main topic's consumer lag, since an unmonitored DLQ is a silently leaking pipeline.

Replay procedure: after fixing the bug, read the message and its metadata from the DLQ, patch the envelope if needed, republish to the original topic keeping the same key, and remove it from the DLQ only once the consumer confirms successful processing.
Seeing the same message twice is normal under Kafka's at-least-once default delivery (redelivery on retry, rebalance, or a consumer crashing mid-processing), not a rare fault.
Making the effect happen only once has to be built at the consumer via idempotency, not fixed at the broker — end result: receive N times, charge exactly once.
The client supplies a unique id on the message, used to recognize a delivery as a duplicate.

Before charging, the consumer does an atomic check-and-set (SETNX-style) on that id, so the second delivery is detected as a duplicate and skipped, even when both deliveries arrive almost simultaneously.
The consumer still keeps a durable unique constraint on the transaction store as the last line of defense, so if the fast marking layer loses its trace, the duplicate insert is still rejected.
A consumer's groupId determines which consumer group it belongs to; consumers sharing the same groupId are members of ONE group.
Kafka assigns each of a topic's partitions to exactly one member within a group, so within that group each event is delivered to only one consumer.
The 5 order-processing workers must share the SAME groupId (e.g., order-processing-group), so orders are load-balanced across them with no duplication.
When a worker joins or leaves the group, Kafka rebalances partition ownership among the remaining/new members automatically.
The analytics consumer must use a DIFFERENT groupId (e.g., analytics-group) than the workers, making it an independent group rather than a 6th member sharing the workers' partitions.
Because it's a separate group, analytics receives its own copy of every partition/event, not a slice of what the workers get.
Kafka does not delete a message once consumed; each group tracks its own private offset (cursor) into the log, independent of other groups' offsets.

Since offsets are per-group, analytics can start from offset 0 (or auto.offset.reset=earliest) to replay the full order history within the retention window, with no coordination or republishing needed from order-service.
The proposal does not work the way the teammate expects — scaling to 12 pods will not yield 4x throughput.
Kafka's assignment rule: each partition is assigned to at most one consumer per group, so a group's number of useful consumers can never exceed the topic's partition count.

On a 3-partition topic, even with 12 pods in the group, only 3 pods ever hold a partition; the other 9 are assigned nothing and sit fully idle, so actual throughput does not increase despite quadrupling the pod count.
To genuinely raise the parallelism ceiling, you must increase the topic's partition count first and then scale consumers alongside it, not just add pods to the existing group.

Increasing partitions is not a free change — it triggers a rebalance and remaps keys to different partitions, breaking the ordering an entity previously had, which makes partition count a decision that needs careful thought, not a dial to turn casually.
"Exactly-once" is actually two different guarantees hiding under the same name.

Exactly-once DELIVERY is really a distributed transaction spanning the broker, the consumer's processing step, and the store, and every participant must commit or roll back together, which is expensive and fragile the moment any participant sits outside that boundary.
For a payment consumer that boundary is broken from the start, because the side-effect that matters is charging a card through an external payment gateway that no Kafka transaction can reach into.
Even a perfect exactly-once-delivery setup would not stop a duplicate charge if the gateway call itself fires twice.

Exactly-once EFFECT accepts that Kafka is at-least-once and redelivery will happen, then blocks the duplicate at the effect layer with a client-supplied unique id claimed via an atomic check-and-set before the write.
A unique database constraint serves as the last line of defense if that check-and-set layer ever loses its claim.
This idempotent-effect approach is cheap and robust because it only needs the consumer and its own store to agree, not a transaction spanning the broker and an external gateway.

Transactional exactly-once still earns its keep for Kafka-to-Kafka stream processing, where the read, transform, and write-back all stay inside Kafka and a real cross-topic transaction is achievable — but it stops being the right tool the moment the effect crosses into an external store or a third-party API.
Doubling numPartitions on a live topic silently breaks the ordering of entities that already have history, without any error or warning surfacing.

The mechanism lives in the partition-selection formula itself: the target partition is hash(key) % numPartitions, so numPartitions is a parameter inside the routing formula, not a config number that sits outside it.
When N changes, hash(key) % N produces a different result for the same key, so existing keys get remapped too, not only keys created after the change.

The concrete consequence is that an entity's older events stay in the old partition while its newer events land in the new partition, and since FIFO is only guaranteed within a single partition, cross-time ordering for that entity is effectively gone.
The core trade-off is that more partitions buy parallelism and throughput, but the price is weakening the ordering guarantee for precisely the keys that already had history before N changed.
A safer fix is to over-provision the partition count up front for ordering-sensitive topics before go-live, instead of bumping N later.
Another safe option is a stable custom partitioner that maps a key to a partition by a rule independent of the current value of N.
If more capacity is genuinely needed, the controlled route is standing up a new topic with the desired N and migrating deliberately, rather than changing N in place on a topic serving live traffic.
Kafka partition routing is determined by `hash(key) % numPartitions`, so the literal bytes of a message's key - not the topic or consumer group - decide which partition it lands in.

An entity's events stay in FIFO order only if the key used to produce them is byte-identical every single time across that entity's entire lifecycle; any change to the key can send it to a different partition.

Building the partition key as `accountId + schemaVersion` makes the key drift whenever schemaVersion changes (for example after a deploy), turning the same account's key from something like `acc-9` into `acc-9-v2`.
Once the key changes, `hash(key)` can map the new key to a different partition than the old one, so a single account's event stream ends up split across two partitions instead of staying in one.

Splitting one entity's stream across partitions breaks ordering because Kafka only guarantees order within a single partition, not across partitions - so a later event such as a withdraw can be consumed before an earlier event such as a deposit if they land in different partitions.
The fix is to key solely on the immutable entity identifier - the raw accountId - and never fold in a schema version, deploy flag, or any other value that can change over the entity's lifetime.
The invariant that must hold for correct ordering is: same entity, same key, same partition, same order.

A regression test for this bug class should emit a burst of events for one accountId while a simulated schemaVersion change happens mid-stream and assert every event lands in the same partition, or that a single consumer reads them back in exact send order.

In this NestJS `@EventPattern` handler, KafkaJS only advances (commits) a partition's offset when the handler's returned promise resolves; any exception thrown out of the handler leaves the current offset uncommitted.

Because `handle` wraps `processEvent` with no try/catch, an uncommitted offset causes the broker to redeliver the exact same message on the next poll, producing an infinite retry loop for that one record instead of ever moving past it.

Kafka guarantees ordering only within a partition and processes records in that partition sequentially, so a message stuck retrying forever blocks every message queued behind it in the same partition — this head-of-line blocking is exactly the observed symptom of climbing lag with nothing else from that partition getting through.

A duplicate `clientMessageId` (the Redis `SETNX` dedup check missing, i.e. `lock !== "OK"`) is not a real failure — the event already succeeded the first time — so throwing `ConflictException` for it conflates a harmless no-op with an actual error and lets it stall the whole partition.

A genuine processing error, such as the `simulateFailure` throw, is a distinct case from a duplicate: it represents a poison message that needs to be isolated for later investigation rather than either endlessly blocking the partition or being silently discarded.

The fix wraps the call to `processEvent` in a try/catch inside `handle`: on a detected duplicate it logs and returns normally so the handler resolves and the offset commits, while on a genuine error it publishes the message to a dead-letter queue topic and then also returns normally so that offset commits too.

Both branches of the fix deliberately end in a normal return rather than a rethrow, because returning (not throwing) is what tells KafkaJS to commit the offset — the fix works specifically by turning both the "not really an error" path and the "handled error" path into a resolved promise instead of a rejected one.

Verifying the fix means sending the same `clientMessageId` twice and confirming only one row is persisted while lag does not climb, then sending a `simulateFailure: true` message and confirming it lands in the DLQ topic while every later message in that partition still gets processed.

A `groupId` built from a runtime-generated value such as `randomUUID()` produces a distinct consumer group on every process boot, and a brand-new consumer group has no committed offset in Kafka no matter how many times the same logical service has run before.

When a consumer group has no committed offset, `subscribe: { fromBeginning: true }` makes it start at offset 0 and read the entire retained log — Kafka is an append-only log that retains messages by a time/size policy rather than deleting them once consumed, unlike a traditional queue broker.

Because the notification-service handler triggers a real-world side effect on each message, replaying the full topic on every restart re-sends notification emails (and re-triggers any other side effects) for orders that were already notified long ago.

This differs from Kafka's genuine intentional replay capability, where a new consumer group is deliberately created to backfill or reprocess data; here the reset to earliest happens as an accidental side effect of a random groupId, not as a deliberate choice by anyone.

The fix is to give the consumer a stable, deployment-independent `groupId` sourced from configuration (a fixed value or an environment variable like `KAFKA_GROUP_ID`), rather than deriving it from per-process identity such as a UUID, hostname, or PID, so restarts resume from that group's own committed offset instead of starting over.

`fromBeginning: true` paired with a genuinely fresh consumer group is appropriate only for a separate, manually-triggered backfill flow, never as the default startup behavior of a production consumer.

Passing tests and running without errors locally does not prove the consumer is correct, because the offset-reset bug manifests only as duplicate real-world side effects across a restart or redeploy, not as a local test failure — so this is a blocker rather than a nitpick.

A senior-style review distinguishes a blocker from a nitpick and confirms intent rather than assuming it — asking the PR author whether the reset to earliest on every boot was deliberate or just a side effect of the random groupId.

Correct behavior can be verified with a restart test: publish and process a batch of events under a stable groupId, restart the consumer against that same groupId, and confirm the second run's processed events do not include any that were already committed in the first run.
